extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military legal officers, commanding officers, War Department officials
extracted.subtask_description: Compiled holdings and administrative rules about Army uniforms, badges, awards, intoxicants, introduction of liquor into Indian country, and principles for statutory and regulatory construction applicable to military administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief of the corps for certificate of merit
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of awarding the certificate of merit, the 'chief of the corps' is the company commander when a Philippine Scout's company is not part of a battalion or regiment; if the company belongs to a battalion which does not belong to a regiment, the battalion commander is the 'chief of the corps'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions C.13978 (Jan.20,1903) and C.16973 (Oct.13,1904) adopt this rule determining whose recommendation suffices for certificate-of-merit awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of merit ineligibility for commissioned officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statutes governing the certificate of merit (section 17, act of March 3, 1847; acts of Aug.4,1854; R.S. sections 1216 and 1285; act Feb.9,1891; act Mar.29,1892), the certificate of merit may not be granted for gallant conduct by a commissioned officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.22110 (Nov.15,1907); statutory scheme prohibits awarding certificate-of-merit for gallant conduct by commissioned officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate-of-merit pay subject to forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Certificate-of-merit pay is part of a soldier's pay and is subject to forfeiture by sentence of a court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.1308 (Apr.30,1895) — award pay treated as pay for purposes of forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'in their own right' for society badges
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'in their own right' in statutes authorizing wearing certain society badges mean entitled because of their own service or because of kinship to one who had been in the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted in C.14956 (Jan.30,1904) as conferring badge-wearing rights by personal service or kinship.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to wear certain society or association badges
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal authority to wear, in uniform, the badge of the Society of Foreign Wars; likewise the insignia of the Association of Military Surgeons may not be worn by officers or enlisted men in uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in decisions cited at C.14956 (Sept.12,1903) and C.15610 (Apr.6,1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: President prescribes uniform and manner of showing service
rubrics_metrics.description: The President prescribes the uniform of officers and enlisted men under section 1296 R.S., and determination of how service in war or particular operations shall be shown (e.g., service stripe or metallic device) is within Executive discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive may indicate service by stripes or metallic devices and prescribe uniform regulations for wearing them (C.23875, C.17243 and related G.Os); Quartermaster Department may procure and issue such devices, either charging clothing allowance or issuing as equipage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster supply and charging of distinctive badges
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartermaster's Department may supply distinctive service badges/devices to enlisted men (charged to clothing allowance or issued as equipage) and to officers at cost price; such badges may not be issued to volunteer officers/enlisted no longer in service (would be a prohibited donation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.23875, C.17243, C.14201 and others; badges treated as stores and supplies per act Jan.21,1903 (32 Stat.775).

rubrics_metrics.name: Badges are stores/supplies and may be issued to governors for Organized Militia
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive badges constitute stores and supplies within the meaning of section 17, act of Jan.21,1903, and thus may be issued to governors of States for use by their Organized Militia as part of the uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement rule for campaign badges
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or enlisted man who served in a campaign recognized by a campaign badge is entitled to the badge if he was in the service at the date when service in that campaign was designated for recognition, or if he was not in service at that date but is now in service he likewise is entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.17243 (Sept.23,1911); entitlement depends on service when designation occurred or current service status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-entitlement when employment assimilated but paid from insular funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Units formed from civilian employees assimilated in essential incidents to Philippine Scouts but paid out of insular funds (not regular appropriations) are not entitled to the Philippine campaign badge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to 'Batson's squadron' in C.17683 (Mar.15,1905): payment source and formal status affect badge entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awarding badge after discharge not barred by leaving Army
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who became entitled to a badge but was discharged before it was awarded should not be barred from receiving the badge due to subsequent departure from the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.18563 (Sept.14,1905) that discharge before award does not automatically bar award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of beverages with appreciable alcohol forbidden on military premises
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of a legislative definition of 'intoxicating liquors,' the sale at post exchanges of a beverage containing an appreciable quantity of alcohol falls within the prohibition of the act of Feb.2,1901.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in cases C.1809J?, C.19521, C.19768, C.23027 (1905–1908); broad construction used to include beverages with appreciable alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beer is an intoxicating drink for purposes of Army statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 17 of the act for increasing Army efficiency (Mar.2,1899), beer is considered an intoxicating drink and falls within the prohibition on detailing officers or soldiers to sell intoxicating drinks in post exchanges/canteens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C.5992 (Mar.,1899).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipment of intoxicating liquors to military reservations not per se prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law forbidding the shipment of intoxicating liquors to military reservations as such, but sale and method of delivery are regulated by statute and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.13829 (Dec.26,1902) — shipments in original packages to bona-fide consignees for their own use are distinguishable from sale/delivery schemes intended for distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliveries in original packages to bona-fide consignees permitted; speculative consignments forbidden
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliveries on a military reservation by railroad/express of liquors in original packages to bona-fide consignees for their own use do not violate the prohibition; general consignments by dealers to be delivered to unknown parties to be paid on delivery would be an infraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in C.14323 (Mar.27,1903) — factual character of consignment and intended recipient matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking orders and delivering small quantities on reservation is violation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person taking orders on a military reservation from enlisted men for whisky in small quantities and then delivering the same constitutes an express violation of section 38 of the act of Feb.2,1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of whether a beverage is 'intoxicating' is left to commanding officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department should not assume determination of whether specific beverages are intoxicating; this is left under regulations to commanding officers, and no fixed alcohol percentage rule exists; practices in prohibition States may serve as guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in decisions C.18094, C.22782, C.23027 and paragraph 357 A.R.,1910 — discretionary, case-by-case approach recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act prohibiting sale does not apply to officers' messes
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibitions on sale/dealing in intoxicants in post exchanges, canteens, or Army transport do not apply to officers' messes established at military posts for accommodation of unmarried officers and others who do not desire individual messes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State law governs portion of joint maneuver camp occupied by State troops; federal law governs when under sole federal occupancy
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Federal Government accepts the use of a State maneuver camp for joint maneuvers, during the period of joint maneuvers the State laws regarding sale of intoxicants govern the portion used by State troops; in portions used by Federal forces or during sole federal occupancy, the Federal prohibition (act of Feb.2,1901) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in G.19983 (June 29,1906) — allocation depends on occupancy and usage during maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint of opium sale to protect military service
rubrics_metrics.description: If unrestricted civilian sale of opium is causing injury to the military service in a Territory, Congress may restrain such sale under its general legislative power over Territories; absent Congressional action, territorial legislature may regulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested in P.30,72 (Feb.,1889) as means to abate injury at Fort Sherman, Idaho.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's authority to license introduction of intoxicants into Indian country is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of July 23,1892 (amending R.S. §2139), the Secretary of War may give written authority for introduction of intoxicating liquors into Indian country but that authority is subject to restrictions (e.g., cannot properly permit introduction into Indian country within a prohibition State with view to sale to enlisted men); he has no general authority to license sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (various C. and P. citations) stress limitation: permits for introduction only in narrow circumstances and not for sale (see numerous cases cited between 1892–1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permits to introduce liquor into Indian country limited to sacramental/hospital/limited medicinal use with safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice permits are granted only where liquor is to be used in connection with the U.S. Army or for sacramental, hospital, or certain private medicinal use where there is guaranty against abuse; sacramental wine permits are granted only on application of a minister and forwarded through ecclesiastical superior or other authentic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out in numerous decisions (C.2399, 2406, 2571, 2795, 1896; 3140, 3404, 3716, 1897; later cases) — expressly excludes permits intended to authorize sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military commanders authorized to arrest and prevent introduction of liquor into Indian country
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 2150 R.S., a military commander may be authorized/directed by the President to arrest by military force and deliver to civil authorities any persons engaged in furnishing liquor to Indians in violation of law; authority to prevent entry includes authority to arrest where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in R.42,192 (Mar.,1879): prevention power implies arrest power to restrain attempts to introduce liquor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to take and destroy spirituous liquors in Indian country (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2140 R.S. imposes a duty upon 'any person in the service of the United States' to take and destroy spirituous liquors or wine found in the Indian country except such as may be introduced by the War Department; however, this does not authorize destruction of private buildings where liquor is stored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in R.31,205 (Feb.,1871) and R.35,350 (Apr.,1874) — duty to destroy liquors but not to destroy private property unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers not 'premises used for military purposes' under prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises occupied by the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers (including branches) are not 'premises used for military purposes' within the meaning of section 38, act of Feb.2,1901, forbidding sale of intoxicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in O.12817 (July 2,1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised Statutes effective upon Presidential approval (date rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revised Statutes are a single act of Congress which, absent special provision, went into operation on the date of approval (June 22,1874); subsequent certified dates of the printed volume fix when contents became evidence of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.36,630 (Aug.,1875) — practical rule on effective date; supplements later published bring revision down to later dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army statutes effective without publication in general orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws relating to the Army embraced in the Revised Statutes became operative as to the Army upon approval by the President irrespective of publication in general orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.36,666 (Sept.,1876) — publication in general orders is not required to make statutes operative on Army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'may' as 'must' in statutes conferring public duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'may' in a statute conferring power upon a public officer is to be construed as equivalent to 'must' or 'shall' where the enactment imposes a public duty or benefits individuals whose rights cannot be effectuated without exercise of the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in Minor v. Mechs. Bk. and applied in E.42,328 (June,1879) and other decisions; context matters (public duty/benefit to rights holders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'authorized' may be mandatory in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'authorized' generally confers discretion, in some statutory contexts 'authorized' should be construed as mandatory or equivalent to 'required' or 'directed' (examples: issuance of backdated commissions; issuance of duplicate discharge certificates; sale of portion of military reservation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in P.58,309 (Mar.,1893) and other cases — statutory purpose and context determine whether 'authorized' is discretionary or obligatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory mode and form must be followed without material variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a statute clearly requires that something be done in a particular mode and form, the mode and form prescribed must be executed without material variance by the officer charged with performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by requirement to erect a bridge according to a designated plan as condition precedent to expenditure (R.28,664, June,1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of time from an act excludes the day of the act
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general principle, where time is to be computed from an act done, the day on which the act is done is excluded from the computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated in G.1084 (Mar.2,1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative history (remarks, reports) not safely followed in statutory construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks by a Member of Congress, reports of committees, etc., cannot be safely followed in construing a statute; reliance on legislative history is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among rules of construction; see Law I.B.6 and accompanying discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army regulations: scope, limits, and non-contradiction with statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Army regulations fall into three classes; they have no statutory sanction as a whole, are null when in conflict with statutes, cannot grant legislative authority or occupy a field already occupied by statute, are not retroactive unless expressly provided, and must be in furtherance of statutes and founded on necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out in Law I.N. REGULATIONS and Law I.B (pages cited) — specific examples include issuance of rations in emergencies and limits on regulatory reach into constitutionally vested areas of Congressional control.
